subsystems.name: Ge/SiGe heterostructure
subsystems.role: confines positive charge carriers (holes) in a thin strained germanium layer, where the qubit lives.

subsystems.name: Gate stack and quantum dots
subsystems.role: metal electrodes on the surface squeeze the buried holes into small puddles holding a single particle each.

subsystems.name: Cryogenic environment
subsystems.role: keeps the device cold enough that thermal noise does not swamp the spin state, and applies a magnetic field.

subsystems.name: Electrical control
subsystems.role: microwave and fast baseband pulses rotate and couple the spins.

subsystems.name: Readout
subsystems.role: converts a spin state into a measurable electrical signal.
parts: superconducting microwave resonator for dispersive sensing

subsystems.name: Epitaxy and fabrication line
subsystems.role: the growth and patterning tools that make the heterostructure and its nanoscale gates.
parts: molecular beam epitaxy or chemical vapour deposition reactor

buildSteps.title: Grow the heterostructure
buildSteps.detail: On a silicon wafer, a graded silicon-germanium buffer is grown to relax the lattice mismatch, then a thin germanium layer is deposited under strain, capped with silicon-germanium. The strained well ends up tens of nanometres below the surface.

buildSteps.title: Make contact to the holes
buildSteps.detail: Alignment marks and p-type ohmic contacts are patterned, so that reservoirs of holes can be supplied to the dots from the sides.

buildSteps.title: Deposit the gate stack
buildSteps.detail: A thin dielectric is grown or deposited, then nanoscale gate electrodes are written by lithography and lifted off as a metal film — often two or more stacked gate layers to allow overlapping control.

buildSteps.title: Form and tune quantum dots
buildSteps.detail: At cryogenic temperature, positive voltages on the gates pull a two-dimensional hole gas into the well, then pinch it off into small dots. Charge-stability measurements confirm that each dot holds exactly one hole.

buildSteps.title: Calibrate spin control
buildSteps.detail: A microwave burst on a gate drives electric-dipole spin resonance, tilting the hole's motion so its spin flips. Rabi oscillations and gate fidelities are measured and the pulse shapes corrected.

buildSteps.title: Couple two qubits
buildSteps.detail: Neighbouring dots are pushed together so the holes' wavefunctions overlap, giving an exchange interaction; a voltage pulse then implements a two-qubit gate.

buildSteps.title: Add a resonator and scale up
buildSteps.detail: A superconducting microwave resonator is fabricated alongside the dot array for dispersive readout and for linking distant qubits, and the same layout is repeated across a wafer so that fabrication statistics can be measured.

buildSteps.title: Industrialise the process
buildSteps.detail: The whole stack is transferred to a large-wafer foundry flow, with cryogenic control electronics placed near the qubits to cut down the number of wires running into the refrigerator.

prerequisites.why: natural germanium contains a spin-carrying isotope, so the quietest material has to be grown from purified source to get long spin coherence.

prerequisites.tech: Low-defect epitaxy of germanium on silicon
prerequisites.why: the two materials have a large lattice mismatch, so buffer engineering is needed to bury the dislocations far from the quantum well.
dilution refrigerators are commercially available, but wiring and cooling power limit how many qubits one machine can host.
dots need gate features of a few tens of nanometres with tight overlay between layers.
resonators and near-quantum-limited amplifiers developed for superconducting circuits can be reused.
room-temperature instruments cannot scale to large arrays; multiplexing circuits operating near the chip are still being developed.

pathway.milestone: single-hole and two-hole qubits in academic laboratories, with fast all-electrical single-qubit control and coherence times long enough for thousands of gate operations
pathway.unlocks: a credible materials platform for semiconductor spin qubits.

pathway.milestone: small arrays of several coupled dots with on-chip readout and two-qubit gate fidelities approaching the fault-tolerance threshold
pathway.unlocks: the building blocks for a logical qubit made of many physical spins.

pathway.milestone: fabrication on mature large-wafer silicon lines with cryogenic control chips
pathway.unlocks: hundreds of qubits per chip, made with the yield and uniformity of the semiconductor industry.

pathway.milestone: error-corrected spin-qubit processors, possibly hybridised with superconducting resonators or photonic links between chips
pathway.unlocks: a scalable quantum computer built in a foundry rather than a laboratory.
